problem: The intent node says why flightcrew exists and what it is. It does not say what this second attempt leaves behind, or why the first attempt's result is not it. Ground: the built system is 12,579 lines, 68% runner and check libraries; its 30 suites pass at HEAD; the sources put the human at three gates reading evidence and writing the diagnosis afterwards. The ten registered problems name what is wrong. One sentence fixes what the end-to-end proof exercises and what the critic judges the diff against.

questions.text: What is the outcome of this run, in one sentence?
questions.why: This becomes the intent's outcome clause. The test-builder derives the end-to-end proof from it and the planner decides what the last wave must leave behind. Each option makes a different thing primary.

options.value: A run of flightcrew conducts itself: from a frozen spec under launch/<name>/, hooks, workflows and sealed dispatches carry the run through its gates and produce a record whose every line is recorded, not stated, and the human's part is reading at three gates and writing the diagnosis after.

The foundation: every artefact a run reads or writes is a schema-governed JSON document at a fixed address under launch/<name>/, freeze lives in the document, and the runner is reduced to leaf tools; conducting a run end to end is the next launch's outcome.
Flightcrew builds its own next version: the outcome is a run, conducted by flightcrew, that lands flightcrew-core v3.

questions.answer: custom: flightcrew runs under its own power for the first time; the human corrects the first run's mistakes and keeps its accepted foundations; a simpler but just as effective system leveraging files and Claude Code tooling far more.

questions.text: Why is the first attempt's result not the outcome? Pick the reason the intent should carry.
questions.why: The intent's why clause. The run log, the plan's risks and the critic's reading all lean on this sentence when deciding whether a defect is in scope. The three options are the three roots the problem set traces to; only one can be the headline.

options.value: The system never ran itself: both recorded runs were driven by hand and transcribed into its format, so nothing it claims about a run has been observed.
The runner became the system: the spec described its commands, the tests tested the CLI, and the human advanced a run by typing.
The human's judgement was bypassed: the diagnosis was written by the agent, the map revised mid-run, the next run opened before the last was closed.

questions.answer: custom: v1 was built by a dynamic workflow that created its own spec and prioritised a fully testable command surface as the driver; this time the human assumes their intended role and dispenses their vision for a simpler, more native, just as capable system.

questions.text: At the end of this run, what must you be able to do that you cannot today?
questions.why: Acceptance is written last but it is anchored here: this is the thing the owner confirms. The options differ in how much of a real run must happen in front of you.

options.value: Start a run against a small fixture spec and watch it proceed to gate one without typing a state command; approve; watch it reach the end; read a report whose provenance is recorded; write the diagnosis; and have the next run refuse to open until it is written.
Open any launch folder and, from its JSON documents alone, know the run's phase, what is frozen, what each role was handed and what it returned, without a command.
Hand the frozen v3 spec to the crew and have it build it, with me at the gates only.

questions.answer: custom: the infrastructure exists for every element of a run — valid spec, tests, kickoff workflows, plan units, agent roles, build, verify, adversary, merge, review, write results, record events, log, cleanup — proven as infrastructure, not by an end-to-end run with a replacement human.

questions.text: What is this run's stance toward what is built and green today?
questions.why: Decides whether the spec is written as a revision of an existing system or as a definition the existing files must be made to fit. It shapes every scope node: what the implementers may keep, what they must not rebuild, and what the critic treats as pre-existing.

options.value: Revise: everything a registered problem does not name is kept as built, and the spec names what stays so no unit rebuilds it.
Redefine: the spec states the system from scratch; whatever built code satisfies a node is reused by the implementers' choice, and the spec does not name it.
Rebuild: v1's code is reference only; the new system is written fresh beside it and v1 removed when the run lands.

questions.answer: custom: revise — the spec condenses what exists and expands what does not; problems orient the questions, they name nothing.
